pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Electromagnets

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics, 'Magnetism'):** 'the magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets, D.C. motors (principles only)'.

- **Standards — US (NGSS, MS Forces & Interactions — MS-PS2-3):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-3] — the clarification statement explicitly names 'the effect of the number of turns of wire on the strength of an electromagnet' (DCI PS2.B; assessment of quantitative questions limited to proportional reasoning).

- **Operational details:** The new idea: magnetism can be CREATED by an electric current — a current-carrying wire has a circular field; coiling the wire adds the loops' fields into a bar-magnet-like field (solenoid); a soft-iron core concentrates it. Its defining feature is that it can be switched ON/OFF and varied, unlike a permanent magnet. Pupils INVESTIGATE the three strength factors (current, number of turns, soft-iron core) as a controlled fair test — qualitative/proportional reasoning, NOT quantitative field-strength calculation.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B→C (early-formal, age 12-13).
bestPractices: Build the idea in the sequence single wire → coil → cored coil: a current makes a circular field around a wire; coiling adds each loop's field; a soft-iron core greatly strengthens it.
Foreground the defining advantage — an electromagnet is switchable on/off and adjustable in strength — and anchor it in real uses (scrapyard crane, relay, MRI, maglev).

Investigate the three factors as a controlled fair test: change current OR turns OR core while holding the others constant; measure strength by paperclips lifted (or a force meter); take repeat readings.
Vary current safely with 0/1/2/3 cells in series rather than a power pack (which overheats the wire); demonstrate if needed.
Insist on precise language: 'turns' are loops added to ONE coil (not 'more coils'), and the wire must be INSULATED so the current goes round every turn rather than shorting across touching turns.
Use a SOFT-iron core (magnetises and demagnetises instantly) and explain why steel (a 'hard' magnetic material) is wrong — it would stay magnetised and not switch off.
keyRepresentations: Single straight wire with a circular field shown by plotting compasses around it
Coil/solenoid with a bar-magnet-like field; the classic nail-and-coil electromagnet
Fair-test results table: factor varied vs strength (paperclips lifted)
Cells-in-series to step the current; turns counted compactly along one core
Real-device images: scrapyard crane, relay, MRI, maglev
commonMisconceptions: 'Turns' means 'number of coils' — turns are loops on a single coil (Oak).
A magnetic field is the same as the electric field around a charged object — a charged balloon does NOT deflect a compass, but a current-carrying wire does (Oak).
Bare/uninsulated wire is needed for the coil — insulated wire is needed so the current loops each turn (Oak).

Faulty causal stories for why paperclips fall off when switched off ('the magnetism returns to the power pack', 'the wire overheated', 'the clips repel') — the cause is simply no current = no field (Oak).
Any metal core (e.g. copper) will strengthen it — it must be ferromagnetic soft iron; ties to the wider 'all metals are magnetic' error (Oak).
Confusing the MEASURE of strength (paperclips held) with a CAUSE of strength.

learn.summary: Learners aged 12–13 build and investigate an electromagnet to understand that magnetism is created by an electric current, that the magnet can be switched on/off and varied (unlike a permanent magnet), and that its strength depends on current, number of turns on a single coil, and a soft-iron core. The core sequence is a controlled fair-test investigation (change one variable at a time, measure strength by paperclips lifted, take repeats) using qualitative/proportional reasoning rather than quantitative field calculation. A hands-on coil-winding kit with a force meter is the fullest form; a live-state interactive bench is a strong digital stand-in, with diagnostic questions, a labelled reference image, and an optional coil-winding sandbox as supporting layers.

activities.title: Electromagnet test bench: isolate what changes the strength
feedback: When current stops, the current-produced coil field stops. A suitable soft-iron core usually loses most induced magnetisation, unlike a harder magnetic material that retains more; inspect the actual result rather than treating retained clips as proof that current was not the field’s source.

Switching off stops the current-produced coil field; it does not send magnetism back to the supply or make the clips repel. Compare the actual switch-off result, allowing for small residual core magnetism.

Compare measured strength with soft iron and copper or no core. Soft iron supplies substantial ferromagnetic strengthening in this chosen apparatus, while copper does not; the current-carrying coil still has a field in every case, and whether it lifts a clip depends on its strength and the setup.
If a learner says 'more coils' instead of 'more turns': turns are extra loops added to ONE coil; count them along the single core.
If two variables were changed in one run, point out you cannot tell which caused the change — repeat with only one varied.

Soft iron is chosen because it magnetises readily and typically retains little magnetisation after the applied field is removed. Harder magnetic materials such as steel can retain more, making clean switch-off less effective; test the actual core rather than promising instant complete demagnetisation.
activities.rationale: A live, manipulable bench lets learners isolate each of the three factors and witness the switch-off drop, directly confronting the named causal misconceptions (stored magnetism, any-metal core, voltage vs current) while practising fair-test logic. The strength relationships and the fair test are well captured in a 2D live-state model; a real kit adds the enquiry craft of winding, noisy measurement and repeat readings.
sourceClaims: MS-PS2-3: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-3]; clarification explicitly cites the effect of the number of turns of wire on the strength of an electromagnet; DCI PS2.B — electromagnetic force sizes depend on currents/magnetic strengths and distances.

A current in a wire makes a magnetic field; coiling adds the loops' fields; a soft-iron core strengthens it and lets it switch on/off (steel would stay magnetised). Strength rises with more turns, greater current, and a soft-iron core. Named misconceptions: turns vs coils; magnetic vs electrostatic field (charged balloon doesn't deflect a compass); needing bare wire; faulty reasons for clips falling; copper core working. Vary current safely with cells, not a power pack.
KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: the magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets, D.C. motors (principles only).
learnerActions: Build the electromagnet: wind insulated wire around a soft-iron nail and connect it to cells so it picks up paperclips.
Before switching off, predict out loud what will happen to the dangling paperclips the instant the circuit is broken, and WHY.

Switch the current off and observe how many paperclips fall or remain. The current-produced coil field disappears; a suitable soft-iron core usually loses most induced magnetism, but residual core magnetism or sticking can leave some clips attached.
For the current test, keep turns and core fixed and use teacher-approved current-limited settings. Measure the current and record paperclips lifted at each setting, with repeat readings.

For the turns test, keep the core fixed, add turns to the same coil, and check the measured current stays fixed using the approved controls; otherwise note current as a confounding change. Record repeat strength measurements.

For the core test, hold measured current and turns fixed and compare soft iron, copper, wood and no core. Record the actual paperclip counts or compass response. The current-carrying coil produces a field without iron; soft iron normally strengthens it substantially, while copper and wood do not provide that ferromagnetic strengthening. Do not predetermine that the core-free coil cannot lift a clip.
Each run, change only ONE variable; if more than one is changed, note it as a confounded run that cannot show a single cause.
Optionally overlay plotting compasses or a compass near the coil to show the solenoid's bar-magnet-like field.
activities.intendedInsight: Current produces the coil’s magnetic field, which can be controlled by switching or changing the current. A soft-iron core strengthens the field and usually retains little magnetisation after switch-off. Strength depends on current, turns and core material; changing one measured variable at a time helps isolate a cause.

activities.title: Build the idea: single wire → coil → cored coil, and real uses
feedback: If a learner claims a single straight wire has no field: a compass placed near a straight current-carrying wire deflects (Oersted); coiling just concentrates the field.

If a learner treats the magnetic field as the same as the field around a charged object: a static charge produces no magnetic field, while a current produces a steady circular magnetic field round the wire. Any slight pull of the needle towards a charged balloon is electrostatic attraction, not magnetism.
If a learner thinks bare wire is needed: the wire must be INSULATED so current goes round every turn instead of shorting across touching turns.
For real uses, tie each example back to current-based control — the crane drops its load by cutting the current, while devices such as MRI and maglev rely on strong current-controlled fields.
activities.rationale: Building the concept in the single wire → coil → cored coil sequence grounds why each stage increases strength and separates magnetic from electrostatic effects, while real-device anchoring makes the current-controlled advantage memorable. A labelled reference image with tap-to-reveal parts and a real-uses gallery supports vocabulary but, being static, cannot run the fair test or show the switch-off drop, so it complements rather than replaces the bench.
sourceClaims: A current in a wire makes a magnetic field; coiling adds the loops' fields; a soft-iron core strengthens it and lets it switch on/off (steel would stay magnetised). Strength rises with more turns, greater current, and a soft-iron core. Named misconceptions: turns vs coils; magnetic vs electrostatic field (charged balloon doesn't deflect a compass); needing bare wire; faulty reasons for clips falling; copper core working. Vary current safely with cells, not a power pack.
KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: the magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets, D.C. motors (principles only).
learnerActions: Hold plotting compasses around a single straight current-carrying wire and observe the circular field around it. Compare with a charged balloon: a static charge produces no steady magnetic field. A strongly charged balloon can still tug the needle slightly by electrostatic attraction, but it does not make the steady circular pattern around the wire that the current does.
Coil the wire and observe how the loops' fields add to make a bar-magnet-like field (a solenoid).
Add a soft-iron core and observe the field strengthen.

Match real devices to magnetism CREATED and CONTROLLED by an electric current — scrapyard crane, relay, MRI, maglev — explaining the control each relies on: the crane and relay most clearly switch the magnet on and off, while MRI and maglev depend on strong, current-controlled fields that can be set or varied.
Explain in your own words why a scrapyard crane can pick up AND drop a car just by switching the current, while a simple permanent magnet cannot be switched off to release it.
activities.intendedInsight: Magnetism can be CREATED by a current; coiling concentrates it and a soft-iron core strengthens it, and the defining advantage over a permanent magnet is being switchable and adjustable. A magnetic field (from current) is distinct from the electric field around a static charge.

activities.title: Diagnose causes and vocabulary: why did the clips fall?
feedback: Stopping current removes the current-produced coil field, which is why a suitable soft-iron electromagnet usually releases its load. Magnetism is not returned to the supply, and the clips do not drop because they suddenly repel; real cores may retain a little magnetisation.

A soft-iron (ferromagnetic) core increases strength; a copper core (like no core) does not give that strengthening. It leaves only the coil's own field, which is usually much weaker but may still lift clips if the current and turns are large enough.
On voltage vs current: field strength is set by the current through the coil; adding cells raises current (and voltage together), so credit the current rather than voltage alone.
A core-free coil with current still produces a field. Soft iron strengthens that field and usually loses most induced magnetisation after disconnection, though some residual magnetism may remain.
Distinguish the MEASURE of strength (paperclips held) from a CAUSE of strength (current, turns, core).
activities.rationale: Diagnostic questions that reuse the documented faulty-cause distractors give precise retrieval and formative assessment of the targeted misconceptions. These check understanding rather than build the investigation, so they are best used alongside the hands-on/interactive work rather than instead of it.
sourceClaims: A current in a wire makes a magnetic field; coiling adds the loops' fields; a soft-iron core strengthens it and lets it switch on/off (steel would stay magnetised). Strength rises with more turns, greater current, and a soft-iron core. Named misconceptions: turns vs coils; magnetic vs electrostatic field (charged balloon doesn't deflect a compass); needing bare wire; faulty reasons for clips falling; copper core working. Vary current safely with cells, not a power pack.
learnerActions: Answer a diagnostic question on why the paperclips fall off when the current stops, choosing between faulty-cause explanations ('magnetism returns to the power pack', 'the wire overheated', 'the clips repel') and the correct 'no current = no current-produced coil field (a soft-iron core keeps only a little residual magnetism)'.

Sort proposed changes into those that DO and DON'T increase strength (e.g. more current, more turns, soft-iron core vs copper core); and address 'voltage-only' reasoning by noting that strength is set by the current through the coil (adding cells raises both voltage and current together).
Fill in the key vocabulary: turns, insulated, soft iron.
Predict whether a coil with current but NO iron core would still deflect a compass, and whether the nail stays magnetic after disconnection, then justify each answer.
activities.intendedInsight: The current produces the coil field; turns are loops of insulated wire on one coil. A soft-iron core is a useful strengthening material with low retained magnetisation, but the core-free coil still produces a field and may lift clips if sufficiently strong.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain and probing discussion
feedback: If a learner expects the nail to stay strongly magnetic, test it after switch-off: a soft-iron nail usually keeps only a little residual magnetism, while a steel nail may keep more. If a learner expects a bare coil to do nothing, run the bare coil (or a straight current-carrying wire near a compass) to show current alone makes a field; the soft-iron core amplifies it.
If a learner credits voltage not current: current is the rate of flow of charge, and the field depends on the current through the coil.
If a learner denies a straight wire has any field: the Oersted demo shows a compass deflecting under a straight current-carrying wire.
Full response: field produced by current (switchable), core concentrates but isn't the source, and strength relates to current, turns and core — applied to the crane picking up and dropping a car.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain cycle with targeted probes is a strong way to elicit and confront the specific errors documented here, especially the discriminating 'remove the core' test. It is a teaching and assessment routine rather than a quantitative investigation and pairs naturally with the bench work.

Strength rises with more turns, greater current, and a soft-iron core. Vary current safely with cells, not a power pack.
learnerActions: Predict what happens to the paperclips the instant the battery is disconnected, and WHY, before carrying it out.
Predict whether the coil ALONE (nail removed) can deflect a nearby compass, then test it.

Answer probing questions: would the core-free coil still affect a compass and why; name one change that strengthens it and one that doesn't and why; why can a scrapyard crane pick up AND drop a car; what actually produces the field — the metal, the battery, or the moving charge?

Explain that current produces the coil field and switching current off removes that contribution; a soft-iron core strengthens the field and usually retains little magnetisation. Relate measured strength to current, turns and core material.
activities.intendedInsight: Committing to a prediction then testing it surfaces the 'iron-is-the-magnet' and 'voltage-not-current' ideas and pins the field to the moving charge; learners should be able to transfer the reasoning to real devices like a scrapyard crane.

constraints: Keep reasoning qualitative/proportional: investigate how strength depends on current, turns and core, not quantitative field-strength calculation (consistent with the age range and MS-PS2-3's proportional-reasoning limit).

Use a teacher-approved low-voltage, current-limited classroom circuit and its instructions. Cells and power supplies can both overheat a low-resistance coil; adding cells is not inherently safe. Keep practical tests brief, disconnect between readings and stop if wire or cells warm.
Use INSULATED wire so current goes round every turn instead of shorting across touching turns; count 'turns' as loops on a single coil, not 'more coils'.

Use a suitable soft-iron core to demonstrate substantial strengthening and usually little retained magnetisation after switch-off. Steel may retain more magnetisation. Copper and wood lack the ferromagnetic strengthening of soft iron, but a current-carrying core-free coil still produces a field and can lift clips if current, turns and geometry suffice; observe actual strength rather than hardcoding a no-lift outcome.
Fair testing requires changing only one variable at a time with repeat readings; a confounded run (two variables changed) cannot attribute a change to a single cause.

A static labelled image supports vocabulary and real-use anchoring but cannot run the fair test or show the switch-off drop, so the causal and investigative learning needs the hands-on kit or the live interactive bench. A 3D coil-winding sandbox adds spatial/building experience but the strength relationships are captured in 2D; treat it as optional enrichment, not the core teacher.

A real coil-winding plus force-meter kit adds enquiry craft (winding, noisy measurement, repeats) that a simulation only models; where feasible accompany or precede the digital bench with the physical investigation.
Distinguish the MEASURE of strength (paperclips held or force-meter reading) from the CAUSES of strength (current, turns, core).
Field strength is set by the current through the coil; attribute strength to current (adding cells raises current and voltage together), not to voltage alone.
Anchor real uses to current-created, current-controlled fields: the crane and relay clearly switch on/off, while MRI and maglev rely on strong controllable fields rather than routine on/off toggling.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The Oak National Academy source is marked verified:false in the row; treat its specific misconception list and safety guidance as informative but unverified. The DfE and NGSS sources are marked verified:true.

Claims in the legacy recommendation that a static image 'cannot teach' the causal/investigative content, that no conversation persona can advance the investigation, and that the live sim is uniquely suited have been softened to scoped affordances/limits; comparative efficacy or necessity is not established by the source claims here.

The statement that a bare coil (no core) 'still works' as a magnet is physically sound (a current-carrying solenoid produces a field), but ensure in practice the current/turns are sufficient for an observable compass deflection; a weak coil field may be hard to detect otherwise — hence the detectability is now qualified in the activity text.

Whether 'voltage does not affect strength' was imprecise in the original candidate: the field depends on current, and adding cells raises current and voltage together, so the teaching point is that current is the direct cause — reflected in the sort and feedback.

MRI/maglev are retained among real uses but reframed as current-controlled fields rather than simple on/off examples, since an MRI magnet is not routinely switched on and off; the crane and relay remain the clearest on/off illustrations.

assess.poeTask: Build the coil-and-nail electromagnet lifting paperclips. Ask students to predict what happens to the clips the instant you disconnect the battery, and WHY, before doing it — then predict whether the coil ALONE (nail removed) can deflect a nearby compass. Predicting the nail 'stays a magnet' or the bare coil 'does nothing' reveals the iron-is-the-magnet idea; the observations pin the field to the current.
probeDeeper: If you removed the iron nail and had just the coil with current flowing, would it still affect a compass? Why?
Name one change that would make the electromagnet stronger and one that wouldn't help, and say why.
Why can a scrapyard crane use an electromagnet to pick up AND then drop a car, when a permanent magnet couldn't?
What actually produces the magnetic field here — the metal, the battery, or the moving charge?
assess.correctAnswer: The magnetism comes from the electric current flowing in the coil — a current produces a magnetic field. Stop the current and the field disappears, so the nail is no longer magnetised and the clips fall. Without the iron nail the coil alone still makes a (weaker) magnetic field when current flows; the iron core just concentrates and strengthens it — it is not the source.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The iron nail is really the magnet — the coil and battery just wake it up.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run the bare coil (or hold a compass near a straight current-carrying wire) to show current alone makes a field; the soft-iron core only amplifies it.
errorPatterns.distractor: The iron nail is really the magnet; the current just switches it on.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expects the nail to stay magnetic after disconnection, and says a coil with no core wouldn't be magnetic at all.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It's the voltage that makes it magnetic, not the current.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach current as the rate of flow of charge; the field depends on the current through the coil.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes field strength solely to voltage and can't name current as what matters.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A straight current-carrying wire has no field — you need it coiled to get any magnetism.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the Oersted demo: a compass under a straight current-carrying wire deflects; coiling just concentrates the field.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that a single straight wire deflects a nearby compass.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the iron core is the magnet (expects it to stay magnetic, or nothing without the core), or attributes strength only to voltage.
responseLevels.full: Explains the field is produced by the current (so it vanishes when current stops, hence switchable), the iron core concentrates but doesn't cause it, and relates current, turns and core material to strength — transferring to why a scrapyard crane uses an electromagnet.
responseLevels.partial: Lists the three factors (current, turns, core) and says it switches on and off, but treats these as separate facts — can't explain that the CURRENT is the source (so the field goes when current stops) or that a bare coil still works.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I wrap a coil of wire around an iron nail and connect it to a battery — it picks up paperclips. When I disconnect the battery, the paperclips drop off. Why does the nail lose its magnetism when the current stops — and would it still work if I took the iron nail out and left just the coil?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The switch-off behaviour separates 'the current is the source' from 'the iron is the magnet'. A student who thinks the iron core is the magnet expects it to stay magnetic (or can't explain why the clips drop) and expects nothing without the core. A student who understands electromagnetism attributes the field to the current, so it vanishes when current stops and a bare coil still works. Tier 2 (remove the core) is the clincher.
